title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
subtitle: Watch one overloaded server get fixed two ways, a bigger box or more boxes, and see what each choice costs.
learn: The difference between scaling up (vertical) and scaling out (horizontal)
Why a single big machine has both a hard ceiling and a single point of failure
How adding servers behind a load balancer raises capacity and survives failures
Why cost per request served often rises at the top of the instance range
When a bigger box is the right and simplest answer, especially for databases

steps.title: One server is running hot
steps.body: Your shop runs on one 4 vCPU server that can handle about 800 requests per second (an assumption for this lesson). Traffic has doubled and now peaks at 680 requests per second, so the CPU sits at 85 percent. Latency starts climbing well before CPU hits 100 percent, so 85 percent is already uncomfortable, and one more good week will mean queueing and timeouts. You need more capacity. There are two basic moves.
steps.idea: Capacity problems have two fixes: make the machine bigger, or add more machines.
steps.caption: Peak load is close to the server's limit.

steps.title: Scale up: a bigger box
steps.body: Vertical scaling means replacing the server with a larger one: more CPU cores, more RAM, faster disks. Here you move from 4 to 16 vCPU. Capacity rises roughly four times, to about 2,800 requests per second (a bit less than 4x because of contention). Cloud prices in this range grow about in line with size, so cost goes to about $600 a month. Your code does not change at all.
steps.idea: Scaling up is the simplest fix because the application stays exactly the same.
steps.caption: Traffic now goes to one much larger server.

steps.title: The limits of one machine
steps.body: Keep scaling up and you hit walls. Suppose you grow to a 64 vCPU instance: about 9,000 requests per second (not the 12,800 that 16x the cores would suggest) at about $2,400 a month. Cloud price per vCPU stays roughly flat as you go up, but each extra core adds less throughput (locks and shared memory), so the cost per request served climbs. Very large or memory-heavy machines, and buying your own hardware, can also cost more per core. Resizing usually needs a restart, and the one box is still a single point of failure: if it dies, the site is down.
steps.idea: Scale up has a hard ceiling, rising unit cost at the top, and no protection from failure.
steps.caption: A 64 vCPU box in the same slot is still one failure away from an outage.

steps.title: Scale out: more boxes
steps.body: Horizontal scaling adds more machines of ordinary size and spreads the work across them. Here a load balancer fronts three 4 vCPU servers. Capacity is about 2,400 requests per second for roughly $450 of servers plus about $20 for the load balancer. Adding a fourth box later adds another 800, so growth is in small, cheap, reversible steps. The catch: your app must work when requests land on different servers.
steps.idea: Scale out grows capacity in small steps by adding ordinary machines behind a load balancer.
steps.caption: The load balancer now fronts three servers.

steps.title: Work is shared
steps.body: Each request lands on one of the three servers, so each carries about 227 requests per second, around 28 percent CPU. Every server talks to the same database, which is where shared data lives. For this to work, servers must not keep user state in local memory, or the next request may land somewhere that does not know the user. That design (statelessness) and the balancing rules are covered in their own lessons.
steps.idea: Scale out works when any server can handle any request, so state must live outside the servers.
steps.caption: All three servers read and write one database.

steps.title: One server dies
steps.body: Now server 2 crashes. The load balancer notices through health checks and stops sending it traffic. The remaining two servers handle about 1,600 requests per second, well above the 680 you actually have, so users see nothing except maybe a few failed requests during detection. Spare capacity beyond peak, often called N+1, turns a hardware failure into a non-event. The single big server could not do this. The balancer itself must also be made redundant, which the load balancing lesson covers.
steps.idea: Many small servers survive failures; spare capacity is what makes that survival real.
steps.caption: Server 2 fails, the other two absorb its traffic.

steps.title: What scale out costs you
steps.body: Horizontal scaling moves complexity from hardware into software and operations. You need a load balancer, health checks, deployment across many machines, and fleet monitoring. Each added server also adds overhead (more network hops, more to deploy), so gains are slightly under linear. Scaling out lets the app tier take three times the traffic, but every server talks to the same single database, and each opens its own connection pool, so total connections grow with fleet size. The database becomes the next bottleneck; scaling data out is much harder than scaling stateless code.
steps.idea: Scaling out adds operational and design complexity, and shared data stores become the next bottleneck.
steps.caption: Three servers now funnel into one database.

steps.title: When the bigger box wins
steps.body: A relational database is the classic case. It keeps data consistent in one place, and splitting it across machines is hard, so the usual first move is a larger instance with more RAM to keep hot data in memory. Small products also win with one box: at 680 requests per second, one mid-size server, perhaps with a standby, is simpler to run than a fleet. Scale up first while it is cheap and easy, then scale out when you hit the ceiling or need availability.
steps.idea: Scale up first for databases and small systems; scale out when you need failure tolerance or outgrow one box.
steps.caption: The database node is the one to make bigger first.

steps.title: Pick by the constraint
steps.body: Scaling up is simple and needs no code change, but it has a ceiling, rising cost at the top, and one point of failure. Scaling out adds capacity in small steps and survives failures, but requires stateless services, a load balancer, and a plan for shared data. Most real systems do both: scale the database up first (later adding read replicas), and scale the stateless app tier out.
steps.idea: Scale up for simplicity, scale out for headroom and resilience, and combine them.
steps.caption: Both paths shown: one big box and a pool of servers.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the main weakness of scaling up a single server, even a very large one?
options: It always requires rewriting the application
It has a hard ceiling and remains a single point of failure
It cannot use more than 4 CPU cores
It makes the database slower by definition
quiz.why: A bigger box needs no code change, but there is a largest machine you can buy, and if that one machine fails everything it serves goes down.

quiz.q: You run three servers, each at 75 percent CPU at peak. One fails. What is the most likely result?
options: Nothing changes because load balancers add capacity
The other two run near 90 percent, which is tight but workable
The other two need about 112 percent each, so they overload and requests fail
The failed server's traffic is automatically dropped
quiz.why: Three servers at 75 percent carry 2.25 servers' worth of work. Two servers can only supply 2.0, so they cannot keep up. This is why N+1 headroom matters: size the fleet so peak load still fits after losing one.

quiz.q: Your stateless web tier is at its limit and you must keep serving if one machine fails; your single database is at 40 percent CPU with room to spare. What is the sensible first move?
options: Add more web servers behind the load balancer
Shard the database across four servers
Replace the web tier with one very large server
Switch the database to a different vendor
quiz.why: Several stateless servers give more capacity and survive a single failure; one big server would still be a single point of failure, and the database has headroom so sharding adds complexity for nothing.

quiz.q: A team wants to scale a primary relational database for the next year with minimal risk. Why is a larger instance often a good first choice?
options: Databases cannot run on more than one machine ever
Bigger instances are always cheaper per core
Scaling out is impossible in the cloud
It keeps data in one place with no new consistency problems and needs no application changes
quiz.why: A single primary avoids splitting data and the coordination problems that follow. Scaling up is often the simplest path until you outgrow it, though replicas and sharding exist for later.

cheatsheet.def: Make one machine bigger with more CPU, RAM, or faster disks. Simple, no code change, but has a ceiling and one point of failure.
Add more machines and spread work across them. Grows in small steps and tolerates failures, but needs stateless design and a load balancer.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down. One big server is the typical example.
Keep enough spare capacity that losing any one server still leaves you above peak load. A rule of thumb, not a guarantee.
Cloud price per vCPU is roughly linear with size, but capacity gains flatten at the top, so cost per request rises. Specialty and on-prem top-end hardware can also cost more per core.
Scale up first while it is cheap and simple. Scale out the stateless tier when you need headroom or resilience. Scale databases out last (read replicas first, sharding last).
